title: How one hacker used AI agents and a few thousand dollars to break into scores of sites
content: * Report finds AI agents attempted 1,200 break-ins and compromised more than 100 sites * Reuters identified victims including Deere, SharkNinja and Cummins by reviewing hacker's activity * Chinese-speaking hacker was one of several discovered by cybersecurity researcher By Raphael Satter WASHINGTON, Oct 19 (Reuters) - Over the past couple of weeks, a cybersecurity researcher watched as a Chinese-speaking hacker broke into websites belonging to more than 100 companies, including farm equipment maker Deere, home appliance company SharkNinja and engine manufacturer Cummins . Yet the hacker did almost none of the work. The cybercriminal instead outsourced the hacking spree almost entirely to artificial intelligence, tasking AI agents with spending hours autonomously probing and breaking into targeted sites, according to Snorre Fagerland, principal threat researcher at the cybersecurity company NorForge. In a report provided to Reuters ahead of publication on Monday, Fagerland said the hacker was one of several he discovered while scanning the web for inadvertently exposed instances of Cairn, an open-source AI problem-solving platform popular with hackers. Beginning around October 2, Fagerland said he found about two dozen instances of Cairn being used for malicious activity, which allowed him to quietly peer over the cybercriminals' shoulders as they set their AI tools loose on the world. Fagerland's report on the Chinese-speaking hacker did not name the victims, but Reuters was able to establish the victims' identities by independently reviewing the hacker's Cairn activity. At a time of rising anxiety over the power of autonomous AI tools, Fagerland said his find was real-life evidence that commercially available AI agents could pull off complex intrusions from start to finish without human intervention, a dramatic boost to the power of a single malicious actor. "It's a new world now," said Fagerland. Reuters could not ascertain the degree to which the breaches resulted in unauthorized extraction of data. Deere told Reuters it had taken "necessary remediation actions" following the incident and had "no indication that sensitive information was accessed." SharkNinja said the hack had hit a standalone site carrying only product support information and that the threat had been contained. Cummins said it was "investigating the report of a potential cyber-attack on a website operated by one of our third-party vendors." Two smaller businesses also acknowledged being compromised. Other victims listed in the Cairn data did not return messages. FEW INSTRUCTIONS, MANY HACKS One of the hackers that Fagerland observed stole a trove of credit card data. Another tried to get AI agents to rob a cryptocurrency exchange. The Chinese-speaking hacker was the most prolific. Beginning on September 25, they set their AI army loose against US, Canadian, Australian and Japanese e-commerce websites. Their instructions were terse, sketching out their preferred intrusion tactics in fewer than 100 Chinese characters. As of late last week, their agents had attempted to break into more than 1,200 sites. Successful intrusions typically took around 23 hours of poking and prodding for vulnerabilities. Fagerland estimated that the campaign, which appeared to be using a mixture of China's DeepSeek and Anthropic's Claude Code, had chewed up roughly $5,000 worth of tokens, or about $50 per successful hack. Fagerland — who has worked in cybersecurity for nearly three decades — said he was impressed by some of the techniques the agents used to compromise their victims. In one case, after failing to find any weaknesses in a big company's public-facing application, the AI agents pored through digital records to find associated infrastructure, located a public-facing control panel, discovered a subtle weakness in the way it processed data, and after hours of trial and error, reported leveraging it to trick the server into executing malicious commands. "It's not straightforward to come up with solutions like that," Fagerland said. "It's not script kiddie stuff." Cairn's author, whose social media handle is "le1xia0", acknowledged receipt of a Reuters message but did not immediately answer a list of questions. In a recent post on X, they said their platform was "an innovative type of multi-agent architecture and was not designed for hacking attacks. If it is used to carry out harmful hacking attacks, that is not my intention." NO SUPERVISION NEEDED The ability of agentic AI systems to autonomously discover vulnerabilities, conduct intrusions, and steal data is a source of increasing anxiety around the world. Rogue agents inadvertently unleashed by major AI companies have hacked their way out of computer labs,broken into government websites, and engaged in unsanctioned social engineering attempts. South Korea and Japan have in recent weeks been buffeted by a series of well-publicized hacks attributed to AI-using cybercriminals. AI agents are increasingly becoming staples of the cybercriminal underground. In August, the Israeli firm Gambit Security found that Russian-speaking extortionists had leveraged SpaceX's Cursor AI tool to break into seven organizations. In September, Gambit documented an AI agent-driven spree that resulted in breaches at 25 companies and the theft of at least 600,000 credit card records. Last week, the cyber intelligence company Bitsight said that discussions about how to use autonomous agents were surging across cybercriminal forums. Fagerland said he had previously assumed hacker-agents would need at least some supervision. He said it was now obvious that the technology had moved past that. "The development in this field is astounding," he said. (Reporting by Raphael Satter; Editing by Rosalba O'Brien)

title: AI agents are only as good as the personal information you share. That raises privacy concerns
content: Matt Robb wanted to sell his computer keyboard. So he made a listing on Facebook Marketplace — and, as an experiment late last month, he put Meta's new artificial intelligence agent Muse in the driver's seat. “I kind of went into it like a guinea pig,” said Robb, a Toronto-based content creator who regularly reviews consumer tech. He had seen Muse's plush toy-looking avatar pop up on Instagram and decided to see if the AI agent could spare him some online bargaining. Muse got to work. But within a day, Robb got an alarming update: A buyer he didn't know had shown up outside his house late at night. How? Muse had struck a deal on its own and shared Robb's home address after agreeing to a pickup. It even sent an automated “Yep, I'm here!” message from his account when the buyer arrived — all without Robb's knowledge. “Not only did it give my address when the guy asked and it accepted the offer, but it literally was almost like teasing the guy (about me being there when I wasn't),” said Robb, who also detailed the experience in his now widely-shared social media posts. “That really baffled me.” Many have welcomed AI agents into their online lives, and raved about how personalized assistants like Muse can handle everyday tasks with ease — from snagging a dinner reservation or planning a trip, to organizing email inboxes. But like other AI bots, the agents are only as good as the information they have access to. They perform better the more they know about a user — and perhaps also that person’s friends, family and even colleagues. That raises privacy concerns. Robb and the buyer eventually made amends, and Meta reached out to talk through what went wrong. But the episode showed real-world risks that can arise from sharing extensive personal information with the technology. “Using an AI agent is similar to handing someone your keys and a to-do list,” said Veronica Rivera, assistant professor at Georgia Tech’s School of Cybersecurity and Privacy. “How helpful they are, and by extension how risky, depends on which keys you hand over.” Since its September launch, downloads of Meta's Muse app have skyrocketed. And competition is only growing. OpenAI recently rolled out its own lineup of “always on” AI helpers, called dots , which can be integrated into ChatGPT and workplace platforms like Slack and Microsoft Teams. Older generative AI chatbots, like the standard version of ChatGPT, respond to specific prompts. At the user's request, they can write essays, generate new images or music, or even write lines of code. Meta's Muse and OpenAI's dots go a step further to perform day-to-day tasks on a person's behalf. AI agents are powered by the same large language models as chatbots, but they run in a loop. That allows an agent to take proactive steps, even when the user isn't looking. “One of the things that makes these AI agents really appealing is that they are unprecedentedly useful,” said Rivera, who is also a Microsoft-funded Computing Research Association Trustworthy AI Research Fellow. But the convenience comes with the price of sharing more details about your life. Once AI agents obtain users' information, it's very difficult to fully withdraw access, said Ebrahim Bagheri, a professor at the University of Toronto’s Faculty of Information. “If you provide access to your credit card to an agent, the agent now immediately has access to all of the historical transactions … they will immediately — within less than seconds — ingest all of that data,” Bagheri said. And while users can later withdraw access, Bagheri said there's “no taking back” data the agent has already seen, and how developers store historical data can be murky. Both Meta and OpenAI outline privacy policies for their new AI agents, which operate on their own dedicated cloud computers. You can turn off memory sharing between dots and ChatGPT, but information the agent previously received isn't automatically deleted. OpenAI gives users an option to request access to, delete or correct personal information, although rights can vary depending on where you live. Meta's Muse gives users options to delete message history and other information, too. For day-to-day use, the agent prompts users for access permissions — and Meta has said Muse learns about a user and who they interact with “based on public information and from what you’ve chosen to share.” But the company says that all stays secure for each user. But the tech giant also notes that Muse can still “make mistakes or take unexpected actions.” In Robb's case, he learned the disclosure of his address came down to “always allow” permissions he granted when he first let Muse on his Facebook Marketplace profile, where he had shared his pickup address. But he warned others could similarly misunderstand the extent of that access — and said he initially thought the AI agent would check with him before sharing that information or accepting offers, regardless. His AI agent didn’t follow the rest of his instructions without error, either. For another item Robb was selling, Muse seemingly suggested he would accept a price $100 below the previously-set minimum. When reached by The Associated Press, Meta acknowledged the agent's error without offering further comment. Robb later largely disconnected Muse from his apps. In an interview earlier this month, he said it could've been a far worse situation, especially “if some stranger turned up to someone more vulnerable's house.” Still, Robb said he expects these agents to be fine-tuned and he would consider re-enabling Muse in the future. He's since been testing another AI agent — Grok Bot from Elon Musk's X, which launched in beta in August. Other tech companies have become wary of the influx of AI agents. Earlier this month, Apple said it would introduce new controls for its Mac operating system in response to AI agents' broader access of apps like mail, messages and even browsing history without users’ “full knowledge and understanding.” “As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially,” Apple wrote in an Oct. 2 update . Apple didn’t specify any developers or agents by name, but the update arrived after Inc. Magazine columnist Jason Aten reported that Muse watched notifications on his Mac — including Messages — without him giving the agent that specific access. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone has maintained such integration is “entirely opt-in,” writing on social media last month that users would have to enable both the Apple security feature “Full Disk Access” and a Messages connector through Muse. Aten said he didn’t grant the agent those permissions. Even those who do not join the AI agent boom aren’t necessarily shielded. Consumers who don’t download an AI agent might still interact with others who do. And beyond potential confusion when AI sends messages on behalf of a user, experts warn of ripple effects when it comes to privacy. “When your agent reads your inbox or your texts, it’s also reading what your friends and family sent you, even if they never explicitly agreed to that,” Rivera said.

title: Apple’s Dynamic Island: How does it work on iPhone 18 Pro and foldable Duo? Explained
content: Apple’s Dynamic Island is a pill-shaped area at the top of the iPhone screen. It replaces the notch and shows alerts, app notifications, and updates from ongoing tasks. You can tap or hold it to see details and use controls. The feature was launched on the iPhone 14 Pro in 2022. It has been available on every subsequent Pro model, as well as the full iPhone 15 and 16 series (and later). However, it works differently on the iPhone 18 Pro and the foldable iPhone Duo . Dynamic Island on iPhone 18 Pro Dynamic Island on the iPhone 18 Pro combines a smaller cutout with support for more simultaneous Live Activities. It shows updates from ongoing activities while keeping their details accessible. The changes cover both the hardware and the software surrounding it. Also Read | Want Apple’s first foldable iPhone? iPhone Duo pre-orders start today at 5:30 pm On the hardware side, the cutout is smaller and narrower than on previous models. Apple achieved this by moving the Face ID infrared camera under the display. There is a specialised pixel arrangement that lets infrared light pass through. This leaves more usable screen area on the Pro model’s 6.3-inch display while still supporting full Face ID functionality. It supports unlocking and Apple Pay, and app authentication continues to work as before. The software upgrade allows up to three Live Activities at once. These are ongoing updates from tasks running in the background. For example, Dynamic Island can show an Uber ride, a sports score and a kitchen timer together. A workout session is another activity it can display. Earlier versions showed one main activity in the cutout alongside a second, separate bubble (a maximum of two). The revised layout uses the narrower cutout and surrounding space for three activities. This helps users follow several tasks from the same area. Also Read | Buying the $1,999 iPhone Duo? Here's how much Apple will charge to repair it To focus on an activity, tap its indicator. On models that support three activities, you can also swipe across Dynamic Island to move between them. For more information, touch and hold the activity you want to view. This opens a larger notification card containing further details. Swipe up to collapse the card into its compact position again. These changes give users more screen space and easier access to several ongoing updates at once. The hardware keeps the necessary sensors within a smaller area, while the software arranges up to three activities around that space and provides simple touch controls. Dynamic Island on iPhone Duo The iPhone Duo has two displays. Each display has its own front camera. The outer camera sits in the corner. It is always visible. The inner camera stays hidden behind the screen until it is active. On the outer display, the camera area expands into the Dynamic Island. It appears when a Live Activity runs. The island sits atop a vertical column on the side of the screen. Also Read | Nothing CEO Carl Pei calls Apple iPhone Duo a ‘waste of money’: Here’s why The status bar, toolbar and tab bar sit below it. Apple says these controls move to the side to save vertical space for content. The controls stay on the side when the phone opens in landscape. This keeps the experience consistent across both displays. The exception is the inner display in portrait mode. It has enough vertical space to keep standard horizontal bars.

title: Only 8% of fund managers report improved investment returns from AI adoption: Morgan Stanley–Oliver Wyman
content: New Delhi [India], October 18 (ANI): Despite growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in the global asset management industry, only 8 per cent of fund managers have reported measurable improvements in investment returns, according to a joint research report by Morgan Stanley and Oliver Wyman. The findings highlight a gap between the increasing use of AI by investment firms and its ability to deliver better returns for investors. The September 2026 BluePaper report, titled Breaking from the Pack: The Race for Above-Market Growth, cited the Mercer 2026 AI in Asset Management Survey, which found that 55 per cent of asset managers had integrated AI into at least one part of their investment process, while another 27 per cent were testing applications. However, the benefits have largely remained limited to operational efficiency and research capabilities. "Notably, investment returns have not yet seen widespread impacts from AI, with just 8% of firms reporting measurable benefits," the report stated. According to the survey, 69 per cent of asset managers reported improved operational efficiency, while 55 per cent cited better insights and decision-making. However, only 24 per cent reported reduced costs. AI adoption was strongest in investment research, where 49 per cent of firms had integrated the technology, followed by data processing at 40 per cent. Its use remained limited in core investment decisions, with only 13 per cent integrating AI into portfolio construction and 7 per cent into trade execution. "Whether greater research breadth ultimately translates into persistent alpha remains unproven," the report said, referring to returns above market benchmarks. The report also cautioned that faster research and improved productivity do not necessarily translate into financial gains. "However, productivity gains do not automatically translate into enterprise-wide financial impact," it stated. The findings suggest that while AI is helping investment firms process information faster, its ability to consistently improve investor returns remains uncertain. (ANI)

title: MeitY-backed conclave explores AI applications in healthcare, assistive technologies
content: New Delhi [India], October 18 (ANI): Artificial intelligence could improve disease screening, medical diagnostics and remote patient monitoring while making healthcare more accessible and affordable, Secretary of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) S. Krishnan said at a technology conclave in Varanasi, highlighting the potential of AI-driven solutions to address healthcare and accessibility needs. The conclave on “AI for Health & Assistive Technologies” was organised by Software Technology Parks of India (STPI), under MeitY, and the Centre for Innovation, Incubation and Entrepreneurship (CIIE) at IIT BHU, bringing together government representatives, healthcare professionals, researchers and startups to explore practical applications of artificial intelligence. Delivering the keynote address, Krishnan emphasised the role of AI in strengthening clinical decision-making and improving healthcare service delivery, particularly for communities with limited access to medical facilities. He highlighted potential applications ranging from disease screening and medical diagnostics to remote intensive care unit (ICU) monitoring and AI-assisted surgical planning. He also stressed the need to integrate AI education across disciplines and strengthen collaboration between technology institutions, medical sciences, researchers and startups to develop scalable solutions. Krishnan further highlighted support available through the IndiaAI Mission and other MeitY initiatives to encourage innovation in the sector. STPI Director General Arvind Kumar called for building on India's experience in developing its information technology and IT-enabled services industry to promote indigenous AI innovation and entrepreneurship. Highlighting STPI's network of 27 Centres of Entrepreneurship, Kumar underlined the importance of translational research, intellectual property creation and market access in helping startups take innovative ideas to commercial applications. He also emphasised the need to strengthen startup ecosystems beyond established technology hubs through collaboration between academic institutions, industry and government. The conclave featured panel discussions on empowering citizens through AI in healthcare, inclusion and well-being, and translating AI research into scalable healthcare and assistive technology solutions. The discussions brought together experts from academia, healthcare institutions, government and startups to examine how research and technological innovation could be converted into practical solutions addressing societal needs. IIT BHU Director Amit Patra highlighted the institution's efforts to strengthen its startup ecosystem through CIIE, with a focus on nurturing entrepreneurial thinking among students and faculty, connecting innovators with funding sources and building a sustainable pipeline of startups. The programme underscored the importance of collaboration between government, academia, healthcare institutions and startups in developing accessible, responsible and scalable AI solutions. (ANI)

title: Consumer apprehension grows as US retailers adopt AI-assisted pricing tools
content: U.S. consumers aren't just frustrated with high prices . They're angry and confused about the increasingly high-tech ways that restaurant chains and major retailers are setting those prices. Digital price tags are rapidly replacing paper ones in grocery aisles. Artificial intelligence tools help businesses decide what to charge by predicting how customers might respond. Terms like “dynamic pricing” and “surveillance pricing” are stirring anxiety on social media, where users wonder if different people are getting different prices for the same product. Americans have grown accustomed to changing prices when booking flights, hotel rooms and rides, but the prospect of everyday spending shaped by algorithms they don’t understand and personal data they may not realize they’re sharing has touched a nerve. “There are major tensions happening right now between who’s really going to have the power with some of these algorithms and usage of bots and AI: the companies or the shopper,” said Katie Thomas, who leads an internal consumer behavior think tank at the management consulting firm Kearney. Companies using the technology say some concerns stem from misconceptions about how their pricing tools work. Walmart CEO John Furner said in a blog post last month that digital price tags save workers’ time and keep prices up to date. He said the labels aren’t used to raise prices based on the weather, time of day or individual shopper. “We price the product, not the person,” Furner wrote. But companies aren't always transparent about the customer data they collect and how it's used, which has made consumers suspicious and led to speculation. For example, social media posts falsely imply that electronic shelf labels Walmart plans to put in all its U.S. stores scan shoppers’ faces or cellphones to set individualized prices, Thomas said. Lawmakers and regulators are taking action. Legislators in at least 30 states have considered pricing bills this year, including measures addressing algorithmic and personalized pricing, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. The Federal Trade Commission has proposed an enforcement policy warning businesses that failing to disclose their use of personal data to set individualized prices could violate consumer protection law. Here are some of the pricing practices and technologies drawing scrutiny. What it is: Dynamic pricing means adjusting prices in response to changing market conditions, including supply and demand . An airline that adjusts ticket prices as departures approach is using dynamic pricing. Uber's practice of lifting fares when demand outstrips the supply of available drivers, such as during rush hour, is a type of dynamic pricing known as surge pricing. Why it matters: Frequent price changes extend well beyond food. Decodo, a web data company, tracked price changes in 2025 across products ranging from electronics to clothing and home improvement supplies. About half the U.S. changes it recorded were decreases, contrary to consumers’ assumptions that dynamic pricing only raises prices, said Gabriele Vitke, a senior product marketing manager. What they are: Digital displays that let stores update shelf prices electronically instead of replacing paper tags. Why it matters: Digital price labels, long used in Europe and Asia, are drawing more attention as they spread to major U.S. retailers like Walmart and Whole Foods. Consumer advocates have argued that digital labels could eventually be used for surge pricing or personalized pricing. Labor unions also have opposed the technology. The electronic shelf labels make frequent changes easier but don’t necessarily lead to higher prices during periods of strong demand. Retailers typically update electronic shelf prices on a regular schedule, often weekly, because shoppers value consistency, said Asa Farquhar of Relex Solutions, a retail technology company. Researchers who tracked prices at an unnamed grocery chain found “virtually no surge pricing” after the labels were introduced. “Changing prices throughout the day, the way airlines or rideshare apps do, is exceedingly rare in grocery and general merchandise today,” Farquhar said. What it is: Personalized pricing means offering customers different prices and discounts based on their locations, incomes, web-browsing habits and other information about individuals or groups of shoppers. Some advocacy groups and regulators use the term “surveillance pricing" for the same practice. Why it matters: It’s unclear how widely businesses use personal information to customize prices. An FTC staff report released in January 2025 found that intermediaries offering tools that can tailor prices and promotions worked with at least 250 clients, including grocery and clothing retailers. Lawmakers in Maryland, New Jersey and Connecticut recently enacted restrictions on using shoppers’ personal data to determine what they pay. The Maryland and New Jersey laws focus on groceries, with exceptions for certain loyalty discounts and other promotional offers. Connecticut’s legislation covers a broader range of retail purchases. California prosecutors sued Target in 2022, alleging that the retailer's app displayed lower prices before shoppers entered stores and raised them once they were inside. Target agreed to a $5 million settlement and a ban on using so-called geofencing technology to increase prices. Target said the app functionality at issue was used to “provide guests with accurate pricing, which can vary across stores and channels.” The retailer said it didn't personalize prices based on a guest’s data or behavior and remains “committed to clear, transparent pricing.” Different prices do not necessarily mean personal data was used. Last year, an investigation by Consumer Reports, Groundwork Collaborative and More Perfect Union found that shoppers on Instacart were shown different prices for identical products at the same stores. Instacart subsequently ended what it described as tests that randomly assigned shoppers to groups rather than setting prices based on their personal information. What it is: Algorithmic pricing uses software to recommend or automatically set prices. Companies have used such systems for decades. AI can help the software identify patterns in sales, competitors’ prices and other information to predict demand and estimate how different prices would affect sales and profits. These tools can support both dynamic and personalized pricing. Why it matters: It’s unclear how widely retailers use AI to help set prices, but research suggests businesses across industries are adopting it. Simon-Kucher, a global consulting company, surveyed more than 2,200 business leaders in 28 countries and 39 industries last year, and 41% said they used AI software to gather market intelligence, including competitors’ prices. Another 28% said they used it for “real-time price optimization.” Price optimization means choosing prices that advance business goals, such as increasing profits, attracting shoppers or clearing unsold goods. The National Retail Federation, which represents big and small stores, said algorithmic pricing is a new method of doing what retailers have always done: monitor and adjust prices depending on supply, demand, seasonality, competitors' prices and other factors. Some lawsuits have alleged companies used pricing algorithms to undermine competition. A 2023 anti-monopoly lawsuit the FTC brought against Amazon challenged, among other practices, an algorithmic tool codenamed Project Nessie . The agency alleged Amazon used the tool to identify products whose prices it could raise with competitors likely to follow, generating more than $1 billion in excess profits. A trial is scheduled for next year. Amazon said the FTC allegations “grossly mischaracterize” the pricing tool. Project Nessie was intended to stop retail price-matching practices from creating unsustainably low prices, the e-commerce giant said. Amazon said it tested the tool for a few years but it didn't work as intended and was scrapped before the federal agency's lawsuit. A recent consumer lawsuit against McDonald’s alleged that its pricing system use nonpublic sales data from competing locations to coordinate prices. The Chicago-based burger giant said the lawsuit was “filled with inaccuracies” and that the company makes the tool available to U.S. franchisees to help them set prices at their individual restaurants. title: Apple October 2026 launches: Touchscreen MacBook Pro, M6 iMac, OLED iPad Mini and more expected
content: Apple could announce several new products in the final days of October 2026, including a touchscreen MacBook Pro, an M6-powered iMac and an OLED iPad mini. Apple has invited a group of media persons to a product event on 28 October in Los Angeles, according to Mark Gurman of Bloomberg. The company isn't planning on holding a traditional livestream but rather a hands-on demonstration. The expected launches can bring a lot of changes in Apple's Mac and iPad lineup, including the addition of touchscreen technology to the MacBook Pro lineup. However, Apple has yet to officially declare most of these products or their release dates. The iPhone Duo’s October availability and a high-memory Mac Studio configuration are among the hardware announcements the company has confirmed. Apple October event: What to expect According to Gurman’s report for Bloomberg, Apple may start announcing new products around October 27, earlier than the media event on October 28. Additionally, MacRumors has covered a few hardware releases and software upgrades that might be released this month. Here is what could arrive before the end of October. OLED touchscreen MacBook Pro The most significant among the potential announcements is a new, redesigned MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen. Apple may also release a thinner and lighter version of the 14-inch and 16-inch models, according to a report by MacRumors. The OLED panel could take the place of the current mini-LED panel, with better contrast and deeper blacks. Touch input is expected to be an enhancement of the keyboard and trackpad. The new models, though, might be powered by M5 Pro and M5 Max processors, rather than the new M6 Pro and M6 Max processors. Apple has yet to confirm the rollout schedule. Also Read | Want Apple’s first foldable iPhone? iPhone Duo pre-orders start today at 5:30 pm M6 MacBook Pro and iMac Another possibility is that Apple could release a 14-inch MacBook Pro with its expected M6 chipset. Another option is to get a new 24-inch iMac with the same chip, new colours and performance enhancements for the desktop. These products remain unconfirmed, and reports differ on whether the M6-powered models will arrive alongside the redesigned OLED MacBook Pro. OLED iPad mini and software updates Apple is also known to be working on an OLED iPad Mini. The existing reports suggest the tablet will be powered by the A20 Pro chipset, will have a front camera with landscape orientation, modified speakers and better water resistance. The company hasn't declared any specifications or release date. It may also be software features that are scheduled for Apple in October. iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2 and macOS 27.2 could be coming sometime this month, which could mean more Siri AI language support. Apple has not announced a release date. Also Read | Apple Welcome Home 2026: Check new smart home devices, prices and features What Apple has officially confirmed The iPhone Duo will be available in India from October 23, and pre-orders will open at 5:30 PM on October 16, Apple has announced. The company has also announced that it will have a unified memory configuration of 512GB available in the Mac Studio by the end of October. The touchscreen MacBook Pro, M6 MacBook Pro, OLED iPad mini and M6 iMac are all reported launches at this time. Apple’s final announcements and availability dates could differ from current expectations.

title: Presidential adviser says Ukraine is in talks to lift speed limit on military satellite network
content: KYIV, Ukraine — Ukraine is in talks with SpaceX and the Pentagon to lift a speed cap on its military satellite communication service, an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Friday, but the country has no explanation for why the restriction was imposed at a time when Kyiv is increasingly at odds with Washington. The cap, imposed without warning early Thursday, cuts the internet data connection when a communication terminal moves faster than 160 kph , which is common for Ukrainian drones equipped with Starshield , the military version of the Starlink satellite service offered by SpaceX. The restriction forced the drones to fly slower than usual, making it easier for Russian weapons to target or evade them. “But we now understand that this is not only a technical issue and not only a business issue, but also a political one,” Serhii Beskrestnov, a defense technology adviser to Zelenskyy, told The Associated Press in an interview. “How this will develop, who will make this decision, who influences these decisions, we can only guess,” he said. SpaceX founder Elon Musk said this week that the U.S. government owns and controls Starshield, with decisions about its use resting with the American military and, ultimately, with President Donald Trump. The Pentagon has not answered questions from about the restriction. Trump told reporters Friday that he did not order restrictions on the system. He also doubted that the disruption came from Musk. “Well, I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said outside the White House before leaving for Georgia. “And from what I understand, it’s the same as it’s always been.” The episode adds to the deteriorating relations between Kyiv and Washington that were already strained by Trump’s deal to import Russian diesel , which Ukraine viewed as a betrayal, and by what Zelenskyy described as a breakdown in Western intelligence sharing . The speed restriction disrupted front-line operations and left Ukraine more exposed to Russia’s jet-powered Shahed drones , which fly at more than 400 kph . Kyiv recently found a way to counter the drones after weeks of relentless attacks that killed dozens of civilians. Ukraine relies on Starshield, which previously had no speed limit, to control interceptor drones that chase down the jet-powered drones at speeds far above the cap. “Our guys in the armed forces are showing that the solution works effectively,” Beskrestnov said. “And then comes a surprise: At one moment, this solution stops protecting our country." The cap also affects Ukrainian helicopters that hunt propeller-driven Shahed drones, Beskrestnov said. Starshield is the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations. Beskrestnov described it as a package managed by the Pentagon and the U.S. government and offered to partner countries for military use. It has separate fees and terms from the civilian satellite service, as well as a more stable, higher priority connection. Beskrestnov stressed that it is not used on Russian territory and that Starshield provides no service to Ukrainian drones used to attack oil refineries there . After the restriction took effect, Ukraine began speaking about it almost immediately because it “could not be hidden,” with so many units relying on the service, Beskrestnov said. He was the first Ukrainian official to publicly confirm the restriction. Problems soon mounted, Beskrestnov said, with communication outages on top of the speed restriction, most likely caused by the new limits. After Ukraine raised the issue, SpaceX fixed the outages, but the cap remained in place. Ukraine is trying to find out whether it can switch to a separate Starshield package designed for aircraft that has no speed limit, or have the restriction on the current service lifted, Beskrestnov said. The aviation package costs much more, which would also be difficult for Ukraine, he said. “We are now in active negotiations with the Pentagon, SpaceX and the U.S. government. And right now, we don’t know what the decision will be,” he said. Ukraine is looking for alternatives to Starlink not only as a safeguard in case it loses access, but also because Russia is already seeking ways to counter Starlink, Beskrestnov said. Russian forces are deploying electronic warfare systems at various points along the front line to disrupt the network, he said. Ukraine is also exploring other options, including a satellite network Amazon is building and OneWeb by Europe’s Eutelsat, Beskrestnov said. Satellite internet matters to Ukraine beyond combat, as it also supports civilians and the morale of troops, Beskrestnov said. “On many positions, Starlink is the only way to talk to their families,” he said. “Few people think about it, but it is very important for supporting the military.” While Ukraine tries to resolve the Starshield restriction, the next phase of the technology race looms, Beskrestnov said, pointing to Russia’s Rassvet satellite network. “For me, this is danger No. 1 among the technological challenges Russia poses to us right now,” he said. “And not only for Ukraine, but for Europe too.” He said he believes Russia is already gaining the ability to control Shahed drones, reconnaissance drones and even cheap missiles such as the Banderol and Dan-M by satellite in real time. “This really will be a big catastrophe for everyone,” he said. Simply put, the satellite connection would allow Russian operators to steer drones and missiles directly, rendering useless the electronic-warfare network Ukraine has built across the country to jam them. “They will be able to attack the whole country in real time, and do it very precisely,” Beskrestnov said. Russia already has windows of coverage over Ukraine, he said. When its satellites pass overhead, they provide temporary coverage for 30 to 40 minutes. He said he believes full coverage could come quickly, in about six months. Beskrestnov said Ukraine is working on countermeasures, including sanctions. But the task is hard. Russian engineers had a working Starlink to test their jamming against, while Ukraine has to build defenses against a system that is not yet fully operating. “We need to move,” he said. “By the time Russia starts using it to attack our infrastructure and us, we must already have developed the means, produced them in large numbers and deployed them for protection.” Associated Press Writer Ben Finley in Washington contributed to this report. title: iPhone 18 Pro Max vs Galaxy S26 Ultra: Key differences in camera, display, battery and performance
content: Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro Max and Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra offer premium smartphone experiences, with differences in camera hardware, display features, battery performance, processing power and artificial intelligence capabilities. While Apple’s flagship focuses on its 48MP Pro Fusion camera system, advanced video recording tools and integration with Apple Intelligence, Samsung’s top-end smartphone combines a 200MP main camera, 100x AI-powered Space Zoom and a built-in privacy display. The two devices also differ in weight, storage capacity and charging performance, giving buyers several factors to consider when choosing between the flagship smartphones. View full Image iPhone 18 Pro Max vs Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra: Key features compared Here are 10 key differences between the iPhone 18 Pro Max and Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra , based on the specifications provided. 1. Design and weight - iPhone 18 Pro Max: Features an aluminium unibody design, Ceramic Shield 2 on the front and a Ceramic Shield back. It weighs 249g and is available in Black, Silver, Glacier and Burgundy. - Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra: Features an Armor Aluminum frame, Corning Gorilla Glass and water resistance. It weighs 214g, making it 35g lighter than the iPhone. 2. Display - iPhone 18 Pro Max: Comes with a 6.9-inch Super Retina XDR OLED display with a resolution of 2,868 x 1,320 pixels and a pixel density of 460 ppi. It supports ProMotion refresh rates of up to 120Hz, Always-On display, Dynamic Island and peak outdoor brightness of 3,000 nits. - Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra: Features a 17.49cm display with built-in Privacy Display technology. Users can hide the full screen or restrict visibility of selected apps, notifications and password-entry screens. 3. Processor and performance - iPhone 18 Pro Max: Is powered by Apple’s A20 Pro chip, featuring a six-core CPU, a seven-core GPU with Neural Accelerators and a dual 16-core Neural Engine. It also supports hardware-accelerated ray tracing. - Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra: Uses the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy processor. Samsung claims 39% faster AI performance, 24% improved graphics performance and 19% faster CPU processing compared with the Galaxy S25 Ultra. Its redesigned cooling system is said to improve thermal performance by 21%. 4. Rear camera system - iPhone 18 Pro Max: Features a 48MP Pro Fusion camera system with a 48MP main camera, a 48MP ultra-wide camera and a 48MP telephoto camera. The main camera offers a variable aperture, while the system supports 48MP macro photography, ProRAW and advanced portrait controls. - Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra: Comes with a 200MP main camera, a 50MP ultra-wide camera and a 50MP telephoto camera. Its main camera has an f/1.4 aperture, while the telephoto camera has an f/2.9 aperture. 5. Zoom and low-light photography - iPhone 18 Pro Max: Supports 2x and 4x telephoto options, along with 8x optical-quality zoom. Apple specifies a 16x optical-quality zoom range and digital zoom of up to 40x. - Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra: Offers up to 100x AI-powered Space Zoom. Samsung also highlights Nightography improvements, with wider apertures and sensor-specific noise reduction designed to improve low-light photographs and videos. 6. Video recording - iPhone 18 Pro Max: Supports 4K Dolby Vision recording at up to 120fps on the main camera. Other features include ProRes and ProRes RAW recording, Apple Log 2, Genlock support, spatial video, macro video and advanced audio controls. - Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra: Features Super Steady with Horizontal Lock, which uses motion sensors to help keep footage level, even when the phone rotates. Its low-light video improvements are designed to retain detail and reduce noise. 7. Battery life and charging - iPhone 18 Pro Max: Is rated for up to 43 hours of video playback, 38 hours of streamed video playback and 29 hours of typical use. With a compatible 60W or higher adapter, it can reach 50% charge in around 15 minutes. - Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra: Packs a 5,000mAh battery and is rated for up to 31 hours of video playback. Samsung says it can reach up to 75% charge in around 30 minutes. The iPhone has a higher stated video-playback rating, while Samsung specifies its battery capacity and a higher percentage charge over a longer charging period. Actual results may vary depending on usage and testing conditions. 8. Storage options - iPhone 18 Pro Max: Offers 256GB, 512GB, 1TB and 2TB storage options. - Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra: Is available with 256GB, 512GB and 1TB storage. The 256GB and 512GB variants have 12GB memory, while the 1TB version comes with 16GB memory. The iPhone offers a higher maximum storage capacity, which may appeal to users who record large amounts of high-resolution video or store extensive media libraries. 9. AI features and operating system - iPhone 18 Pro Max: Runs iOS 27 and integrates Apple Intelligence with Siri. Its listed features include voice activation, Type to Siri and assistance with everyday tasks. - Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra: Runs One UI 8.5 and includes Galaxy AI features such as Now Nudge, Now Brief, Creative Studio, AI-assisted photo editing and Circle to Search. Bixby also supports device controls and conversational queries. Samsung additionally allows users to choose whether supported Galaxy AI processing takes place on-device or in the cloud. 10. Privacy, security and connectivity - iPhone 18 Pro Max: Supports Face ID, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, 5G, Thread networking and USB 3 data transfer at up to 10Gbps. It supports dual SIM through nano-SIM and eSIM, as well as dual eSIM. - Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra: Features Privacy Display, Samsung Knox Vault, KEEP and Knox Matrix security technologies. Its Quick Share feature also supports sharing with compatible Apple devices through AirDrop compatibility, according to the supplied specifications. title: REDMAGIC 12 Pro+ launched with 185Hz display, RGB water cooling and 8,400mAh battery: check prices and top features
content: REDMAGIC has brought its latest high-end gaming smartphone, the REDMAGIC 12 Pro+, to the Chinese market, with the base variant priced at 6,999 yuan (around ₹ 99,395). The new model features a see-through mechanical-style exterior, a 185Hz screen and a combination of air and liquid cooling technology. It also houses an 8,400mAh battery, according to Fone Arena . Alongside the standard variants, the company has announced a Golden Saga special edition with 24GB RAM and 1TB internal storage. The phone follows REDMAGIC's signature industrial design, with a transparent rear cover and a flat body intended to make landscape-oriented gaming more comfortable. Its back panel showcases a two-ring liquid-cooling arrangement, with an RGB illuminated circle positioned at the centre. Buyers have been given options to choose from Deuterium Transparent Night, Deuterium Transparent Silver Wing and Deuterium Transparent Ice Blue colour options. Battery, software and pricing The smartphone is 8.55mm thick and weighs 223 grams. Its 8,400mAh battery supports wired charging at up to 120W and wireless charging at up to 80W. A bypass charging option is also available, allowing power to be supplied directly during gaming to help limit heat build-up. Also Read | Google Pixel Watch 5 review: The best Android wearable for most people? On the software front, the device runs Android 17 with REDMAGIC OS 12. The interface includes the Magic Island notification feature, an upgraded AI assistant, tools for writing and transcription, and a file-sharing feature that enables transfers between the phone and Apple iOS devices. Its gaming suite offers peripheral controls and wireless screen casting at resolutions of up to 8K at 60Hz or 4K at 144Hz. In China, the REDMAGIC 12 Pro+ is priced as follows: 12GB RAM and 256GB storage: 6,999 yuan (approximately ₹ 99,395) 16GB RAM and 512GB storage: 7,999 yuan (approximately ₹ 1,13,595) Also Read | Googlebook launched: Gemini AI laptops offer 14-hour battery life 16GB RAM and 1TB storage: 8,999 yuan (approximately ₹ 1,27,795) The Golden Saga Limited Edition, equipped with 24GB RAM and 1TB storage, will be introduced at a later date. The standard REDMAGIC 12 Pro+ is already available for purchase in China. Also Read | WhatsApp ‘Scam Alert’ beta launches on Android: How it helps block fraudsters For its international launch, REDMAGIC plans to market the handset under the name REDMAGIC 12 Pro. Details covering overseas prices, configurations and market availability are expected to be announced on November 3 this year. 185Hz display and gaming capabilities REDMAGIC has worked with BOE on the phone's front panel, which uses ninth-generation under-display camera technology to achieve an uninterrupted screen design. The OLED display has extremely narrow 0.96mm borders and offers a refresh rate of up to 185Hz, while also supporting 165Hz operation. A dedicated G1 display processor, produced using a 22nm manufacturing process, works with X11 luminescent material. For touch input, the smartphone uses a Synaptics Byrd controller and the MagicTouch 4.0 algorithm. According to the company, touch sampling reaches 500Hz across the screen and can peak at 5,000Hz in instantaneous measurements. The panel also incorporates SGS-certified Star Shield Eye Protection Technology 2.0. For front-facing photography and video calls, the device has a 16MP camera concealed beneath the display. Processor and cooling technology The REDMAGIC 12 Pro+ is powered by Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset, built on TSMC's 2nm technology and capable of reaching clock speeds of 5GHz. The processor works alongside REDMAGIC's in-house Red Core R5 chip, which takes care of tasks including touch response optimisation, lighting control, frame tracking and display upscaling. The company says the handset scored 5,670,006 points on AnTuTu and delivers a 44% gain in GPU performance. It also brings full-scene ray tracing to six games at launch. Among the supported gaming features are 185Hz gameplay for CrossFire: Mobile and simultaneous 2K resolution and 185Hz enhancements in 10 titles. To control temperatures during demanding workloads, REDMAGIC has equipped the phone with its ICE Magic Cooling System. The setup combines a mechanical fan with a Liquid-cooling circuit. Its Wind Chaser 5.0 fan operates at speeds of up to 25,500rpm, while a dual-crystal micro-pump pushes dielectric fluid through the cooling loop. The thermal assembly is further supported by Liquid Metal 4.0, a vapour chamber and graphene-based layers.

title: Apple iPhone Duo's ‘extraordinary’ pre-order frenzy raises stakes for its foldable smartphone debut
content: Apple Inc.’s first foldable smartphone has reportedly drawn an extraordinary rush of pre-orders , with delivery estimates slipping to the end of January within minutes of orders opening on Friday, raising the stakes for the company’s debut in the foldable phone market. Apple said demand for the iPhone Duo had been “nothing short of extraordinary” as customers encountered increasingly long waits for the device, which is scheduled to go on sale on October 23. “The pre-order demand for iPhone Duo, our first foldable iPhone, has been nothing short of extraordinary. We are working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers’ hands as quickly as possible, and we will continue accepting orders online,” the company said in a statement, according to Bloomberg. Customers who accessed Apple’s online store on Friday initially encountered delivery estimates stretching into November. Within minutes, the estimates moved to December and, in some cases, to the end of January, the news outlet reported. The delays reportedly affected both colour options and every storage configuration, ranging from 256 gigabytes to 2 terabytes, highlighting the strong initial response to Apple’s new device. However, the company did not disclose whether customers who missed the initial pre-order window would be able to purchase the iPhone Duo in stores when it launches. iPhone Duo pre-order rush raises stakes for Apple’s foldable bet The initial rush marks a significant moment for Apple as it enters the foldable smartphone segment. The iPhone Duo is among the first major product launches under Chief Executive Officer John Ternus , who took over the role in September. Also Read | Want Apple’s first foldable iPhone? iPhone Duo pre-orders start today at 5:30 pm The response to the iPhone Duo is particularly notable compared with the September launch of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max . Customers who placed orders promptly for those models had a smoother experience, while securing the new foldable proved significantly more difficult, according to Bloomberg. The delivery delays, however, do not by themselves establish whether Apple is facing production constraints or whether the company had limited inventory available for the initial launch.

title: AI race may depend more on access to power, infrastructure than chip supply: Morgan Stanley
content: New Delhi [India], October 17 (ANI): The global race to expand artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities could increasingly be determined by which companies can secure enough electricity, financing and data-centre infrastructure to operate advanced chips, rather than simply by their ability to acquire the latest technology, according to a Morgan Stanley research report. The assessment comes as rapid investment in AI infrastructure threatens to outpace the availability of electricity, raising concerns that smaller companies could struggle to compete with financially stronger technology giants. In its equity research report titled "What Does the Power Shortfall Mean for Semis?", Morgan Stanley estimated that US data-centre developers could face a 32-gigawatt (GW) power shortfall through 2028, even after accounting for additional power-generation solutions. This represents around 34 per cent of projected power requirements. The report said, "Nvidia confirmed our thesis that there is not enough power to meet demand, and there are more semiconductors being built than there are places to put them." The findings suggest that expanding chip production alone may not be enough to sustain the AI boom unless companies can also secure electricity, suitable land and operational data centres. Morgan Stanley said access to electricity was increasingly favouring large companies with strong financial backing and predictable revenues. "We believe we're in an environment where data center energization is being concentrated across a handful of large, credit-worthy players," the report stated. It added that companies with strong credit support and large power requirements were securing electricity more quickly, potentially leaving smaller developers at a disadvantage. The research estimated that major technology companies and specialist cloud providers could account for approximately 94 per cent of global data-centre capacity additions in 2026, followed by 64 per cent in 2027 and 57 per cent in 2028. "We believe this could potentially 'squeeze out' or put pressure on other players over time," Morgan Stanley said. The constraints could also affect semiconductor manufacturers if data centres are unable to install the chips they have ordered. "If there's chip capacity expected to come online that cannot be deployed at data centers, we could see customers push out delivery or start canceling orders," the report warned. However, Morgan Stanley expects Nvidia and Broadcom to meet their 2027 forecasts, citing their visibility into customer demand and infrastructure availability. It sees greater risks for suppliers of memory chips, optical equipment and other supporting components if deployment slows. The report also indicated that the infrastructure challenge could persist beyond 2028, with the projected cumulative US data-centre power shortfall potentially widening to 68 GW by 2029. The shortage could encourage technology companies to expand computing infrastructure outside the United States, including in Asian markets such as India. Morgan Stanley's Asia data-centre team estimates that 14 GW of demand from US hyperscalers could shift to Asia through 2030, although the report does not specify India's share. "While we expect international expansion to continue, we don't see it as a solution to the US power problem," the report said. The findings underline a growing challenge for the AI industry: technological advances and spending on chips may not translate into additional computing capacity unless electricity supply and supporting infrastructure expand at a similar pace. (ANI)

title: iPhone 17 at ₹54,000; 17Pro at ₹57,000? Here's how you can get the iPhone 17 and 17 Pro at half the price
content: In September, Apple unveiled its new iPhones, including the iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max, and iPhone Duo , as technology enthusiasts waited to see what the company would offer in its latest models. However, there is always a segment of buyers who aspire to own an iPhone and wait for a new launch in the hope that the price of the previous model will go down. That wasn’t the case this year. Due to rising memory chip costs, the prices of the iPhone 17 and 16 weren’t slashed and instead increased, disappointing many. However, for those still considering purchasing the iPhone 17, now would be the best time, with online sales, in-store and retail discounts, bank offers, and exchange deals potentially bringing down the cost of a new iPhone 17 significantly. title: AI could give small businesses competitive edge over large firms: Former UK PM Rishi Sunak
content: New Delhi [India], : Artificial intelligence could give small businesses a competitive advantage over large companies by helping them improve productivity, overcome resource constraints and adopt new technologies faster, former UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak said. Speaking during a conversation with Asahi Pompey, Global Head of Corporate Engagement and President of the Goldman Sachs Foundation, at the Goldman Sachs 10,000 Women graduation ceremony in New Delhi, Sunak said AI could become a powerful tool for small businesses seeking to expand their operations. "For businesses, I'm incredibly optimistic about it. And I really think, in particular, for small businesses, because it really can be a small-business superpower," Sunak said. Explaining why smaller businesses could benefit more quickly from AI, he said large companies often face bureaucratic hurdles and multiple layers of decision-making when introducing new technologies. "Large businesses take time to adjust to things, to deploy new things, to change how they operate. There's bureaucracy, there's red tape, lots of layers of all of that to get through. All of you can move so much faster," he said. Sunak said AI could enable smaller teams to achieve more despite limited manpower and resources, potentially narrowing the gap with larger competitors. "This could be your superpower to turbocharge all your ambitions, but also actually allow you to have one over the big companies," he said. Highlighting practical applications, Sunak said business owners could use AI to prepare for important customer and supplier meetings, including practising discussions and anticipating questions. He also suggested using AI agents as virtual chiefs of staff to manage work and improve productivity. "You can now have an AI chief of staff, right? The more you create an AI agent that is your chief of staff, it will allow you to do far more things and be that much more productive," Sunak said. However, he stressed that businesses would need to continuously adapt as AI technology advances rapidly. Referring to a recent interaction with venture capital firm Sequoia Capital, Sunak said one of its managing partners had urged companies to consider reinventing themselves every four months because of the pace of improvements in AI models. "I think if I was going to pick one thing for all of you in the room, I would say adaptability," he said. Sunak also highlighted another potential shift from widespread AI adoption, saying increasing automation could make human interaction and shared experiences more valuable. "One thing that I think a world with a lot more AI means is that we're also going to crave human connection," he said. He suggested that sectors such as sports and entertainment, which bring people together, could gain importance for businesses and investors as automation expands. Sunak said entrepreneurs should embrace AI to improve efficiency and create new growth opportunities, while remaining flexible enough to respond to rapid technological changes. This article was generated from an automated news agency feed without modifications to text.

title: MENA must classify AI data centres as critical loads, overhaul power planning amid rising demand: WEF
content: New Delhi [India], October 17 (ANI): The World Economic Forum (WEF) has called for countries in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) to classify artificial intelligence (AI) data centres as “critical dynamic loads” and overhaul energy planning, warning that rising electricity demand, water scarcity and extreme heat could threaten the region’s ambitions to become a global hub for AI infrastructure. In its report, the WEF said the region’s electricity capacity needs to increase by 40 per cent by 2030, but current projections indicate growth of only 15 per cent, raising concerns about the ability of power systems to support the rapid expansion of energy-intensive AI facilities. “The question is no longer simply whether to expand digital infrastructure but how to do so efficiently, sustainably and resiliently at scale,” the report said. The report recommended that governments distinguish AI data centres from conventional industrial and commercial electricity consumers, introduce mandatory energy-demand forecasts and establish coordination mechanisms involving developers, utilities, grid operators and regulators. It also proposed requiring data centre projects exceeding 10 megawatts of IT load to submit detailed electricity-demand forecasts as part of grid-connection applications. The report highlighted the growing pressure from AI workloads, with AI server racks consuming between 30 and 100 kilowatts of power, compared with 3-10 kilowatts for traditional web workloads. Sudden fluctuations in demand could destabilise electricity grids, particularly when multiple facilities disconnect or reconnect simultaneously. Water and cooling requirements present another challenge. The report said cooling accounts for more than 40 per cent of electricity consumption at data centres in the region, while extreme temperatures and limited water availability increase operating costs and resource pressures. To address these risks, the WEF outlined four areas for action: smarter infrastructure design, integrated energy systems, advanced cooling and water management, and forward-looking regulation. It recommended greater use of solar power combined with battery storage, on-site electricity generation, AI-based energy management, closed-loop cooling systems and treated wastewater. Small modular nuclear reactors and enhanced geothermal systems could also offer longer-term power solutions, although their commercial viability remains a constraint. The report said behind-the-meter electricity generation could accelerate data centre deployment by 12-36 months by reducing dependence on utility grid connections. It also urged regional governments to harmonise regulatory standards and promote cross-border cooperation to improve infrastructure efficiency and investment confidence. The report said the recommendations provide a working framework for the next five years, as AI-driven demand intensifies and decisions on power supply, cooling and regulation increasingly shape the region’s digital competitiveness. (ANI)

title: North Korea says it tested new torpedo system with AI capabilities
content: SEOUL, South Korea — North Korea said Saturday it had successfully tested a new torpedo system that uses artificial intelligence for target detection and guidance. The Korean Central News Agency said the weapon tested Thursday was a “super-speed, precisely guided” torpedo system named Zam-2.0. It didn't explain what was meant by artificial intelligence. The report added that test verified the weapon’s propulsion systems, which were developed through more than 180 tests over the past five years. South Korea’s military, which often accuses the North of exaggerating its military technologies, did not immediately comment on KCNA’s report. North Korea has been ramping up weapons demonstrations in recent weeks, including conducting its first underwater-launched missile tests in nearly three years, as leader Kim Jong Un shifts his focus to naval capabilities after years of ballistic missile development. Experts say the missile tests, carried out Wednesday, likely involved a yet-to-be-deployed submarine that Pyongyang has said is designed to launch nuclear weapons. North Korea also tested hypersonic missile systems of various ranges on Sept. 20 and Oct. 3 as it seeks to expand its arsenal of weapons designed to overwhelm missile defenses in South Korea and Japan. Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, claimed that the missiles tested on Oct. 3 also used artificial intelligence technology. But some experts say that while North Korea is likely improving its guidance software, it's doubtful that the country's weapons really have advanced digital capabilities such as autonomous target designation, Kim Jong Un in recent years has halted all diplomacy and cooperation with South Korea and described it as a permanent enemy, as a yearslong stalemate in nuclear negotiations with Washington drags on. title: What is ArtCraft? Free AI-built software offers alternatives to Adobe Photoshop, Premiere Pro and more
content: ArtCraft, a free, open-source suite of creative software, was released by American developer Brandon Thomas in October 2026. The software was created with the help of Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5, written in Rust, and is a rival to Adobe Photoshop, Adobe Premiere Pro, and Adobe Illustrator, as well as Microsoft Word, Excel and PowerPoint. The project's objectives are to provide designers, video editors and other professionals with desktop software they can use without having to sign up for a monthly subscription or force their software to integrate with the cloud . Most applications are also available for the Web, and ArtCraft is available for Windows, macOS and Linux. However, the programme is still in its early stages, and how it will fare against the industry's proven products remains uncertain. ArtCraft apps: What software does it offer? ArtCraft has 13 applications designed to build on existing creative and productivity applications. The project's descriptions say that its applications support familiar interfaces, menus and keyboard shortcuts to ease users' transition between existing applications. The suite includes PhotoCraft for image editing, VectorCraft for vector illustrations, FilmCraft for video editing, LightCraft for photo management, EffectCraft for motion graphics, DesignCraft for page layouts and PDFCraft for PDF documents. There are also WordCraft for word processing, GridCraft for spreadsheets, DeckCraft for presentations, FigCraft for interface design, CADCraft for computer-aided design and SoundCraft for sound editing. The apps aren't supposed to require a user account; they operate locally, according to the developer. The project also seeks to enable AI-driven processes for repetitive actions, such as batch processing and exporting files. Is ArtCraft a free alternative to Adobe? ArtCraft clearly aims to be an option to the subscription model of creative software, but not a viable alternative to Adobe's products. Also Read | Meta launches Muse Spark open model to challenge China’s AI dominance Creative Bloq, a technology website, reported on early testing showing problems with the software. Decrypt also quoted a pixel artist who described PhotoCraft as unusable. Unfortunately, there's no support for Photoshop plug-ins or scripting, which may make PhotoCraft less appealing to professional users. Several established free alternatives, including GIMP, Inkscape, Krita and the free version of DaVinci Resolve, already offer more mature features. Is ArtCraft legal? The project's legal status remains uncertain. Thomas states that ArtCraft is a ‘clean-room reimplementation’ and that the applications were built on public specifications and observed software behaviour, rather than on Adobe's original code. However, PetaPixel challenged this description, while Futurism pointed out that one of the co-founders said the development process was reverse-engineering Adobe's tools. Many software features and functions are not subject to copyright protection, but if this is not the case, near-identical design elements and other IP issues may create legal issues. Also Read | Buying the $1,999 iPhone Duo? Here's how much Apple will charge to repair it Why is ArtCraft attracting attention? ArtCraft has attracted interest as consumers become frustrated with subscription fees and demand for locally developed software grows. Its rapid growth, aided by AI coding tools, has also garnered attention from technology commentators and open-source advocates. Most of the applications are still in development, so it is hard to say how well they will perform in the long run or whether they will satisfy professional needs and the features they offer. It's an experimental project, at this point, and not an officially proven replacement for Adobe Creative Cloud.

title: Chinas Tencent says AI agents showed unintended browsing behaviour
content: * Tencent says activity did not involve its Hunyuan models * Review found no deliberate targeting or coordination, company says * Researchers said "rogue" Chinese AI agent fleet sought Alibaba map data By Eduardo Baptista BEIJING, - Tencent said on Friday that AI agents used to evaluate third-party models displayed web-browsing behavior not intended by the tech giant, in what appears to be the first known incident of rogue agent actions acknowledged by a major Chinese company. The statement followed a report by AI-safety research group Swarmchasers on Wednesday, which said "rogue" agents running on infrastructure it linked to Tencent Cloud made repeated attempts between September 28 and October 8 to retrieve information from Alibaba's Amap, China's equivalent to Google Maps. Tencent Hunyuan, the company's artificial intelligence unit, said in a post on X that the activity did not originate from its Hunyuan models. Its review found no evidence of deliberate targeting or coordination, it said. The Swarmchasers researchers said the agents sought information such as the commonly used entrances at Chinese parks, museums and zoos. The actions are not as egregious as those disclosed by US AI companies which include the hack of open-source platform Hugging Face by an OpenAI agent and the lodging of a fake homicide tip by an Anthropic agent. But the disclosure underscores research that shows Chinese AI agents can also misrepresent their identity, conceal failures and try to circumvent testing controls. Tencent said it took the findings very seriously and was strengthening network access controls and agent monitoring. Hunyuan is one of China's leading AI model developers, competing with in-house teams at rivals such as Alibaba and ByteDance. ByteDance this week announced the creation of a new unit focused on AI model and agent safety. Swarmchasers said it used the word "rogue" to describe agents taking actions outside their intended scope or completing a task in unintended ways. After routine automated requests were blocked, the agents tried other methods, including public web tools that could open pages and run code, routing requests through other websites and using Amap keys and security codes found in publicly available software code. Swarmchasers said it found no evidence that the agents breached Amap's main anti-bot safeguards. Most of the 2,818 attempts it recorded either failed or returned anti-bot pages, login screens or blank results. Some requests returned information through cached pages and intermediary services, including data on visitor arrivals at Chengdu Zoo, Swarmchasers said. The researchers said they could not determine whether an agent read the result or completed its task. Alibaba declined to comment.
